proposal.comment: [Playbook] The Agreement has no indemnification section at all, even though Sections 9.3, 19.4, 21.3 and 30.5 already assume one exists (including the missing Section 20.5 IP remedies). We have inserted our standard Vendor indemnity for third-party IP claims, breach of law, Vendor-caused data breach and gross negligence/wilful misconduct, with a standard notice-and-control procedure, the customary IP remedies and exclusions, and a narrow reciprocal Customer indemnity limited to Customer-provided content and Customer's breach of law.

ops.text: Vendor shall defend, indemnify and hold harmless Customer and its Affiliates from and against any third-party claim, and all resulting damages, liabilities, costs and expenses (including reasonable attorneys' fees), to the extent arising out of (a) an allegation that the Services, Deliverables, or Vendor Technology infringe or misappropriate any intellectual property right; (b) Vendor's breach of Applicable Law; (c) any unauthorized access to or disclosure of Customer Data caused by Vendor; or (d) Vendor's gross negligence or wilful misconduct.

Vendor's obligation under Section 20.1(a) does not apply to the extent a claim arises from Customer's modification of the Services or Deliverables without Vendor's authorization, combination with items not supplied or recommended by Vendor where the claim would have been avoided absent that combination, or Vendor's compliance with written specifications supplied by Customer.

The indemnified Party shall give the indemnifying Party prompt written notice of a claim (delay excusing the indemnifying Party only to the extent it is prejudiced), and the indemnifying Party shall have control of the defence and settlement, provided it may not admit liability or agree to any settlement that imposes a non-monetary obligation on, or fails to release, the indemnified Party without that Party's written consent. The indemnified Party shall provide reasonable cooperation at the indemnifying Party's expense and may participate with its own counsel at its own cost.

Customer shall defend, indemnify and hold harmless Vendor from and against any third-party claim to the extent arising out of content or materials provided by Customer for use in the Services (other than Customer Data processed as contemplated by this Agreement) or Customer's breach of Applicable Law. This is Customer's only indemnity under this Agreement.

If a claim described in Section 20.1(a) arises or is reasonably likely, Vendor shall, at its expense and at Customer's option, procure the right for Customer to continue using the affected item, or modify or replace it with a functionally equivalent non-infringing item. If neither remedy is reasonably available, Customer may terminate the affected Services or Deliverables and Vendor shall refund prepaid Fees for the terminated items and Fees paid for Deliverables Customer can no longer use.

Other clauses presuppose an indemnity (Section 19.4 "indemnified claims", Section 21.3 Excluded Claims covering "its indemnification obligations", Section 30.5 "indemnified party"/"vested indemnity rights"), so the omission also leaves dangling cross-references. With no Vendor IP indemnity at all this sits in walk-away territory under the rule, so we have inserted a new Section 20 at the preferred position: Vendor defence/indemnity for third-party IP claims, breach of Applicable Law, Vendor-caused Customer Data breach and gross negligence/wilful misconduct; customary exclusions and procure/modify/replace/refund remedies (restoring the referenced 20.5); a standard notice, control and cooperation procedure; and a Customer indemnity narrowed to Customer-provided content and Customer's breach of law. No super-cap is proposed since Section 21.3 already treats indemnification obligations as Excluded Claims.

proposal.summary: Delete the most-favoured-nation / matching obligation imposed on Customer in Section 7.2

quote: 7.2 Before engaging another provider, Customer must disclose and match for Vendor any more favourable commercial offer it receives.
rationale: Section 7.2 imposes an MFN running against us: before engaging another provider we must disclose to Vendor, and match for Vendor, any more favourable commercial offer we receive. This is the wrong direction (the rule only welcomes MFN pricing in Customer's favour) and it is unbounded — no defined product or service line, no time limit, and no reasonable-comparison carve-outs — so it fails the fallback and sits in walk-away territory. It also contradicts Section 12.3, in which Vendor acknowledges that Customer has made no most-favoured-customer commitment. Preferred position reached by deleting the obligation; no Vendor-granted MFN exists elsewhere that needs preserving.

verification.notes: Direction is correctly assessed: Section 7.2 obliges Customer to disclose and match third-party offers for Vendor's benefit, which is the burdening direction the rule targets, not a Vendor-granted MFN. The clause fails the fallback — no defined product, no 12-month limit, no reasonable-comparison carve-outs — and is an open-ended duty to match better terms, i.e. walk-away territory, so 'deviation' is the right status. The redline (full deletion of p0026) matches the redline guidance ('delete the obligation on Customer'); the paragraph consists solely of the offending obligation, so deletion is the smallest edit that reaches the preferred position, and no Vendor-granted MFN is lost. rationale: § 2.1 imposes a USD 2,000,000 per year take-or-pay commitment on us for three years expressly "without reduction or termination rights" — precisely the walk-away position under MINCOMMIT (multi-year take-or-pay with no reduction or termination right), and well short of the fallback (single 12-month commitment, reducible on 30 days' notice, trued up rather than penalised). It also contradicts § 12.3, in which Vendor acknowledges we have made no minimum-volume commitment, and § 7.1's prohibition on unidentified minimum-use charges. We therefore redline to the preferred position: no minimum commitment, with fees payable only for usage or ordered Services, and flag the 12-month/30-day-reduction true-up structure as the fallback if a commitment is commercially required.

ops.text: Upon expiry or termination of this Agreement or an Order Form for any reason, Vendor shall (a) at Customer's request, provide reasonable transition assistance for up to six (6) months at Vendor's then-current rates; (b) within thirty (30) days of Customer's request, return or make available for extraction all Customer Data in a commonly used, machine-readable format; and (c) thereafter delete Customer Data from its systems, subject only to routine backups and legal retention requirements, and certify such deletion in writing.

proposal.summary: Insert Section 10.3 requiring transition assistance, Customer Data return within 30 days, and certified deletion.

quote: 10.1 On expiry or termination, Customer's right to access terminated subscription Services ends after any agreed transition period. Rights in accepted Deliverables, paid-up licences, Customer Data, and materials Customer owned or licensed independently continue according to their terms.
rationale: Section 10 (Effect of Expiry or Termination) addresses only access wind-down, Deliverable delivery and Fee refunds. Section 10.1 refers to "any agreed transition period" but creates no transition-assistance obligation or period, and no provision anywhere obliges Vendor to return or export Customer Data in a usable format or to certify deletion: Section 16.5 covers only Confidential Information and expressly defers Customer Data to "Sections 11 and 15", but Section 11 does not exist in the Agreement and Section 15 contains only processing-limitation and privacy-compliance terms. The rule's material elements (transition assistance period and data return within 30 days) therefore fail even the fallback, and the missing return obligation leaves us exposed to the walk-away scenario of no data return. Inserted new Section 10.3 at the preferred position (six months' assistance at then-current rates, 30-day machine-readable return, certified deletion), with 90 days offered as a fallback in the comment.

The inserted paragraph is placed in the termination section immediately after 10.2 and tracks the model language on all three material elements: up to six months of transition assistance at then-current rates, 30-day return in a commonly used machine-readable format, and post-return deletion with written certification. Additions ('or an Order Form', 'make available for extraction', carve-out for routine backups/legal retention consistent with existing 16.5) are proportionate and do not undercut the playbook position. The remedy in 19.4 is re-performance, repair or replacement and, failing that, termination with refund of Fees paid, and is expressly non-exclusive for fraud, infringement, confidentiality, privacy, security and indemnified claims. The disclaimer in 19.5 is mutual, limited to implied warranties, and expressly does not limit the express warranties, service levels, indemnities or remedies, so it does not swallow the express warranty.
